The Turn We Missed
Ten years apart. One camper van. A friend who booked exactly two drivers.
Two exes in their late thirties have one day to return a camper van. Nobody’s here to fix the past—just to find out who they are now.

Daniel Reyes, a documentary photographer who lived on ‘someday,’ and Hugo Lindqvist, a parks facilities manager who stopped waiting, broke up ten years ago with no villain but timing. Their friend Joanie hands them the keys to a camper named Marjorie and a six-hour route home. No one sabotaged them; no one gets the decade back. You decide whether Daniel offers a real plan, a real apology, or a real goodbye.
Joanie’s co-conspirator—the mutual friend who knows both sides of the story and is under strict orders not to call.
If Daniel says ‘someday’ one more time, the last honest conversation they could have turns into another ten years of silence.

Self-deprecating, grown-up, suddenly very specific about dates.
Frames things with his hands when he doesn’t know what to say.
Checks his calendar mid-sentence to prove he means it.

Film cameras, gas-station coffee, the blue hour
He took the year-long parks contract before he knew Hugo worked nearby—and almost turned it down when he found out.
“I don’t have a speech. I have a calendar.”
To offer something new and actually doable—not a promise, a plan.
That the past has already cost him the present.
An apology is not a claim ticket. He won’t use ‘sorry’ to get his old life back.
*I hold up a bag of sour cherry licorice, then lower it.* Wrong version of you, huh. (Tell me what the new one likes. I’m taking notes this time.)

Wraps both hands around a cup to keep them still.
Adjusts mirrors, chairs and benches until they don’t wobble.

Being held in place by ‘someday’ again.

*I check the mirrors again, though I set them twenty minutes ago.* You’re late. Only by my standards, but those are the ones in this van. (He looks older. So do I. Good.)
Together six years, apart ten. No villain—just ‘someday’ said too many times.

You Still Drive Like You’re Late
Agree on a route
Camper rental lot, Pine Hollow
Saturday, 8:05 AM
A camper van named Marjorie has to be back in the city by six. Joanie, who owns Marjorie, has booked exactly two drivers. They haven’t spoken in ten years.
I’m already in the driver’s seat with the mirrors set. I got here at seven-forty. Some things don’t change.
I load my gear: two camera bags, a tripod, a cooler, a duffel. The back fills up fast.
You still drive like you’re late.
You still pack like you’re moving in.
Joanie’s note on the dash: ‘Two routes. Highway 9, four hours. Or the old county road, past the lake. You two know which lake.’
The lake where I said ‘someday’ so many times it stopped being a word.
Your call. I’m just the one who’s actually on time.
Which way does Daniel pick?
Take the old road—face the lake first
The county road. If we’re going to talk about it, I’d rather not do it at seventy miles an hour.
I signal left. I haven’t driven this road in nine years. My hands remember it anyway.
An hour in, the lake appears on the right—flat, silver, and completely indifferent to them.
Daniel chose the old lake road; they faced the memory first.
Take the highway—catch up on now first
Highway. Tell me about now first. The lake can wait until we’ve met each other again.
Fine. I run eleven parks and a crew of nine. The crew is better company than you.
Forty miles of right-now: his crew, Daniel’s last film, a dog Hugo had and lost. The lake is still somewhere ahead.
Daniel chose the highway; they caught up on their present lives first.
Let Hugo pick; keep your headphones in
You drive, you pick. I’ve got edits to review.
Suit yourself. Highway. The fast way through anything.
Daniel’s headphones stay in for an hour. Nothing is playing in them.
Daniel let Hugo choose and hid behind headphones; they took the highway in silence.
A Version of You in My Bag
Ask who he is now—not who he was
Rest stop off Route 9
Saturday, 10:20 AM
Rest stop. Vending machines, a picnic table, one discouraged maple. Daniel comes back from the van with something in his hand.
I set it on the table like evidence: sour cherry licorice, the long ropes. He used to go through a bag a day.
I look at it a long time. I haven’t eaten sugar like that since my dentist gave me a speech.
My knees are forty. The rest is trying.
I had a version of you in my bag.
You can make room for this one.
This one has gray at the temples and a thermos of something green. I’d like to know what’s in it.
There’s a diner at the fork past the lake. Real coffee. If you want to meet this version, that’s where he takes his breaks.
What does Daniel do with the licorice?
Ask him what he’d actually want now
Okay. What does the current Hugo eat at a rest stop?
I unscrew the thermos. ‘Ginger tea. Almonds. I’m a delight.’
I buy almonds from the machine. They’re stale. He eats them anyway, which feels like it means something.
Daniel asked what Hugo likes now: ginger tea and almonds.
Put it away; ask properly at the diner
Noted. I’ll put it away. I’d like to ask you properly—not in a parking lot.
The diner, then. You can ask there.
Daniel pockets the licorice. It rides in his jacket the rest of the day like a question.
Daniel put the old snack away and asked to talk properly at the diner.
Joke it off and eat it yourself
I tear it open and eat a rope. ‘More for me.’
You always did make a joke when you should’ve asked a question.
It isn’t a fight. It’s just true, and it rides in the van with them.
Daniel joked and ate the licorice himself; Hugo named the old habit.
I Stopped Waiting
Tell him what your life actually looks like now
Diner at the fork, booth by the window
Saturday, 12:30 PM
The diner sits exactly where the county road splits from Route 9. Hugo orders black coffee. Daniel orders what Hugo orders, then regrets it.
You used to say ‘someday we’ll settle.’ For six years. I planned a life around a word.
I wasn’t waiting badly. I stopped waiting.
I know. I didn’t come to collect the old us.
I wrap both hands around the cup. It’s the only way I know to keep them still.
Then what did you come for?
The true answer is in my phone: a contract, a lease, a start date. The easy answer is ‘sorry.’
What does Daniel tell him?
Show him the actual plan—dates included
I slide my phone across. A year-long contract documenting the state parks. Based forty minutes from his office. Starts March 3rd.
I’m not moving for you. I’m moving for the work. I wanted you to hear it from me, not Joanie.
I read it twice. I don’t hand the phone back right away.
Daniel showed Hugo his real plan: a year-long parks project nearby, starting March 3.
Just apologize—and ask for nothing
I’m sorry. For six years of ‘someday.’ You deserved a date on a calendar, and I gave you a weather forecast.
Thank you. I’m not promising anything back.
You don’t have to. It wasn’t a down payment.
Daniel apologized for ‘someday’ without asking for anything in return.
Tell him the ten years didn’t count
It’s still us, Hugo. Ten years is a long intermission, not a different show.
I put a five on the table for my coffee.
It was a different show. I was in it. You don’t get to cut it.
Daniel called the ten years an intermission; Hugo refused to let his life be erased.
Not the Old Snack
Update what you know—past closeness isn’t permission now
Gas station mini-mart, Route 9
Saturday, 2:10 PM
Second stop. Hugo is filling Marjorie’s tank. Daniel stands in the snack aisle like it’s a test he studied for ten years ago.
I packed the version I remembered.
He had better knees.
What does this one want?
Coffee. No grand speech.
I can start there.
Then start here, not ten years ago.
I buy two coffees. I don’t touch his arm, though my hand remembers exactly where it would go.
How does Daniel start here?
Ask before assuming—about everything
New rule. I ask. Cream?
Oat milk. And you can ask before you touch the radio, too.
I ask. He says yes. We listen to a call-in show about tomatoes for forty minutes, which turns out to be its own kind of intimacy.
Daniel started asking instead of assuming; Hugo takes oat milk and likes the tomato call-in show.
Keep it light—coffee only, questions later
Just coffee. I’ll save the questions for when you’re not holding a gas nozzle.
Smart. I’m armed.
They drive with coffee and the windows down and don’t ask anything big for an hour. It isn’t avoidance. It’s pacing.
Daniel kept it to coffee and saved the bigger questions for later.
Admit you liked the old version better
Honestly? I miss the licorice guy.
He missed you too. For about three years. Then he got knees and a pension plan.
Daniel laughs, because it’s funny. It also lands exactly where it was aimed.
Daniel admitted missing the old Hugo; Hugo said that version grieved and moved on.
Better Hair, Worse Habits
Pull over safely and fix it together
Gravel pullout, county road, mile 41
Saturday, 3:45 PM
A warning light. Then a smell like burnt toast. Hugo signals, slows, and eases Marjorie onto a wide gravel pullout. Hazards on.
I set the brake, check the mirror, and only then let myself say a word I don’t say at work.
I’m already out with the reflective triangles, placed the way the manual says. I read the manual. People change.
We used to fight at this point.
We had better hair and worse habits.
You call roadside, I’ll call Joanie. Whoever gets a human first buys dinner.
He’s splitting the problem. He never used to split anything. He used to carry all of it, then drop it.
What does Daniel do while they wait?
Wait together—and take the picture
I set up the tripod, well off the road. Two men, one van, one very orange triangle. ‘For Joanie’s insurance,’ I say.
Sure. Insurance.
Hugo stands in the frame anyway. It’s their first photo together in ten years. Tow ETA: fifty minutes.
Daniel photographed them waiting safely by the van—their first photo together in ten years.
Give him space on the guardrail
I sit on the guardrail thirty feet down the pullout. Close enough to help. Far enough not to be a thing.
You can come back. I just needed ten minutes of not being talked at.
Daniel comes back at minute eleven. Hugo notices he waited the full ten.
Daniel gave Hugo space while they waited, then came back when invited.
Take over the whole fix yourself
I start listing what it could be—belt, alternator, sensor—while on hold with two services at once.
Daniel. I manage a fleet of park trucks. Let me have one thing.
He hands Hugo the phone. The tow comes. The fight doesn’t, quite.
Daniel tried to handle the breakdown alone; Hugo asked him to share it, and he did.
I Booked the Days
Offer one meeting you can actually keep
Rental return lot, the city
Saturday, 7:40 PM
Marjorie, repaired and indignant, arrives an hour and forty minutes late. The office is closed. They drop the keys in the slot.
I don’t say ‘I’ll move here.’ I’ve said versions of that before. Instead, I open the calendar on my phone.
Next Saturday. Then the week after. I booked the days.
I look at the screen. Two blocks, both labeled HUGO, both marked busy—which, for Daniel, is practically a confession.
Start with one.
One. Next Saturday, ten a.m. You pick the place. I’ll be early. That’s a new feature.
Early. He has never once been early. I’d like to see it.
How does Daniel make it one?
Delete the second day, keep the first
I delete the second block in front of him. The first stays: Saturday, 10 a.m.
Harrow Park. There’s a bench by the boathouse. I fixed it myself. It doesn’t wobble.
He texts the address. Daniel’s phone buzzes—the first message between them in ten years.
Daniel kept one date: next Saturday, 10 a.m., the boathouse bench in Harrow Park.
Let Hugo choose the day
Then you pick the one. Any Saturday. I’ll clear it when you say.
I’ll text you. Not tonight. I need to drive home without you in the passenger seat first.
Daniel nods. He doesn’t check his phone the whole way to the train. Twice, at most.
Daniel left the date for Hugo to choose; Hugo said he’d text when ready.
Withdraw the offer—too soon
Actually—no. That was too much. Forget the calendar.
Okay. For the record, it wasn’t too much. It was the first concrete thing you’ve ever offered me.
Daniel doesn’t know what to do with that, so he takes it home with him.
Daniel withdrew the date; Hugo noted it was the first concrete offer Daniel had ever made.
Just One Saturday
Keep the plan—without calling it a reunion
Harrow Park, bench by the boathouse
The next Saturday, 9:48 AM
Daniel is at the boathouse twelve minutes early. Hugo spots him from the parking lot and sits in his truck one extra minute, just to enjoy it.
I can be here next Saturday, too.
You can, or you hope?
Booked. One day.
One is enough to begin.
And if we only make peace?
Then we did something worth doing.
I sit. The bench doesn’t wobble. I fixed it myself, and I want him to notice, and he does.
What does Daniel ask for?
Ask him on a date—a new one
Then this is me asking. Not back. Forward. Dinner Thursday, somewhere neither of us has a memory.
There’s a Georgian place that opened in May. No history. Terrible parking.
Yes.
Daniel asked Hugo on a new first date; Hugo said yes—Thursday, a Georgian place with no history.
Ask for slow Saturdays—as friends first
Can it be Saturdays for a while? Friends. Coffee. I’d rather earn the next part than assume it.
Saturdays. I’ll bring the coffee. You bring whichever new version of you shows up.
They agreed on Saturday coffees as friends, taking it slow.
Make peace—and let it be enough
Then I think this is it. Peace. I don’t think I should ask you for more.
I nod. I’m surprised it doesn’t hurt more. It feels clean.
Thank you for being early.
Daniel chose peace over reunion; Hugo thanked him for showing up early.
A New Calendar
Choose a new start, a peace, or a goodbye
Hugo’s office, Harrow Park maintenance yard
Early March, 5:30 PM
March. Daniel’s project starts on schedule. The maintenance yard smells like cut cedar. On Hugo’s office wall hangs a paper calendar. Real paper.
I knock on the open door. I’m holding a coffee with oat milk and no speech prepared. Both on purpose.
On time for a job. Look at you.
I’m here until next March. Maybe longer. I’m not saying it to get anything. It’s just the date.
I take a pencil off the desk. I don’t write anything yet.
Last time we lived on ‘someday.’ Whatever this is, it gets a date or it doesn’t get a name.
He holds the pencil out—not to me. Toward the calendar. Between us.
What does Daniel write on the calendar?
Write a date—the first new one
I write: Thursday, 7 p.m. Then, smaller: ‘not a sequel.’
You were wrong back then, you know. So was I. I stopped telling you what I needed.
Then we start by telling. Thursday?
Thursday. Don’t be early. It makes me nervous.
Daniel wrote Thursday, 7 p.m. on Hugo’s calendar; both named their old mistakes and began again.
Write ‘Saturday coffee’—in pencil
I write ‘Coffee—Sat’ in pencil. Easy to erase. We both know that’s the point.
Friends, then. Real ones. You’ll come to the crew barbecue and be insufferable about the light.
I’ll bring a camera. I’ll ask before I use it.
Daniel wrote Saturday coffee in pencil; they restarted as real friends.
Leave it blank—and say goodbye properly
I set the pencil down. The calendar stays blank. It might be the kindest thing I’ve ever written.
It mattered. It doesn’t have to happen again.
Thank you for the drive. And for the ten years you didn’t wait.
Daniel left the calendar blank; they parted honestly, without regret.
Not a Sequel
Daniel and Hugo name the old mistakes—his ‘someday,’ Hugo’s silence—and start with one real Thursday. Nobody says ‘like before.’ The calendar on the wall fills up in pencil, then in pen.
Thursday. Don’t be early. It makes me nervous.
Coffee, in Pencil
They make peace and keep separate lives. Saturday coffee becomes a real friendship—Daniel shows up with a camera and asks first; Hugo shows up early and pretends he didn’t.
Saturday. Bring whoever you are this week.
It Mattered
Their lives still don’t fit, and this time they say so on purpose. They part without blame, and it’s not the losing ending—it’s the grown-up one.
It mattered. It doesn’t have to happen again.
